items.title: RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus
items.summary: Vaccines and monoclonal antibody injections are cutting hospitalizations for the respiratory virus.

items.title: Rattlesnakes have personalities too — to venomous effect
items.summary: A snake’s defensiveness might affect how much venom it produces in a laboratory test.

items.title: Iconic first image of black hole holds up to scrutiny
items.summary: Picture produced by fresh analysis of the data that yielded the first-ever image of a black hole outputs the same, ring-like shape.

items.title: Too dry for cacti: extreme droughts could push iconic species to extinction
items.summary: Analysis reveals these plants face severe habitat loss across the Americas — plus, researchers test a new way to diagnose obesity.

items.title: Getting a grasp on the global wildlife trade
items.summary: A study reports that about 107,000 species are traded worldwide, legally or illegally — more than double a previous estimate.

items.title: Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes
items.summary: Efficient catalyst-controlled C–H arylation of arenes

items.title: A guide to Nature Index tables
items.summary: Information on the methodology used in the ranking for the 2026 Nature Spotlight: Energy.

items.title: Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood
items.summary: Mapping the movements of wildlife across the Amazon and other regions to their exposure to human activities can inform protection initiatives.

items.title: Microplastics change the colour of the sea near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch
items.summary: The waters around the zone of floating debris appear greener and bluer on account of high levels of tiny bits of plastic.

items.title: Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus
items.summary: One of Saturn’s rings consists of a diverse population of icy and rocky grains, each with a distinct composition. How this came about might now have an explanation.

items.title: Daily briefing: Should old, bad science be culled from the literature?
items.summary: AI tools that summarize scientific literature are picking up decades-old flawed papers — should they be retracted? Plus, the first image of a black hole holds up to scrutiny and how the Artemis II mission might have disrupted GPS.

items.title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world
items.summary: Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100.

items.title: Extraordinary materials shaped by the principles of complex networks
items.summary: Network science has inspired the design of materials that spread out their deformation when a force is applied, have tunable stiffness and can control vibrational waves.

items.title: DeepMind's ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
items.summary: AlphaGenome 2 can predict the types of cells where a DNA variant is likely to act.

items.title: Proteins that form the nuclear pore barrier move like liquids
items.summary: Nuclear pores control molecular traffic into and out of the cell nucleus. Measurements in living cells, together with molecular-dynamics simulations, show that flexible protein chains that form the selectivity barriers of nuclear pores are highly mobile, and that a sugar modification and the carrier protein importin-β help to preserve this dynamic state.

items.title: How to avoid aliens and live
items.summary: Silence is golden.

items.title: Earth’s early history told by 3.9-billion-year-old rocks from northern China
items.summary: Ancient rocks in northern China reveal that by 3.95 billion years ago, surface-altered oceanic crust had been buried rapidly to depths greater than 50 kilometres and partly melted. This crust was derived from a mantle reservoir that had been left behind when the crust separated from the early mantle as early as 4.3 billion years ago.

items.title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
items.summary: Agricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.

items.title: How I balance my life as a professional surfer and a university researcher
items.summary: Cliff Kapono shares his advice on ways to navigate and grow two different careers.

items.title: Hideki Shirakawa obituary: chemist who showed that plastics can conduct electricity
items.summary: Nobel prizewinner’s accidental discovery led to new forms of materials, light-emitting diodes and solar cells.

items.title: Give biologists the space to be curious, not just better tools
items.summary: Technology is making biological studies more powerful than ever. But people are the real force behind discovery.

items.title: Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?
items.summary: A promising biotechnology company developed a new approach that might treat a rare disease — but its sole employee didn’t do all the work.

items.title: Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health
items.summary: A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

items.title: New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: Blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins
items.summary: The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

items.title: AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?
items.summary: Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is leading a community of interdisciplinary specialists exploring how to make the energy use of artificial intelligence net-positive.

items.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
items.summary: Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

items.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
items.summary: An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

items.title: Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers
items.summary: Scientists are editing microbes to supply more nitrogen to staple crops.

items.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
items.summary: A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

items.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
items.summary: Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

items.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
items.summary: As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

items.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
items.summary: Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

items.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
items.summary: Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

items.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
items.summary: A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

items.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
items.summary: TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

items.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
items.summary: The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

items.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
items.summary: An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

items.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
items.summary: IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

items.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
items.summary: Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

items.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
items.summary: The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

items.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
items.summary: Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

items.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
items.summary: Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

items.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
authors: Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz
items.summary: Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

items.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
items.summary: A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

items.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
items.summary: Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

items.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
items.summary: The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

items.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
items.summary: A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

items.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
items.summary: PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

items.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
items.summary: A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

items.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
items.summary: Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.
